content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: A Schrödinger bridge based model is proposed for Text-to-Speech (TTS) synthesis. The model has two training stages, the first stage is to train a text to mel-spectrogram network and the second stage is to train a mels-pectrogram to waveform network. The two networks are separately trained and connected by an intermediate variable p. The method is evaluated on a public dataset and achieves good results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

The experimental results are overall promising.

The idea of using Schrödinger bridge is novel.

Weaknesses:

The main claimed goal of this work is to propose the first end-to-end TTS model based on Schrödinger bridges. The phrase “end-to-end” has been used to mean a variety of different things in the context of TTS research. However, the model proposed in this work is clearly not an end-to-end model. What an end-to-end model distinguishes itself from other models is that it has no intermediate representation, such that, all the parameters can be jointly optimized using a single network. However, the proposed model consists of two separate networks, the first network produces a latent variable p from the text sequence and the second network produces the output by inputting with p. The a latent variable p is an intermediate representation and the parameters of the two networks are optimized separately. There are some end-to-end TTS models that also have more than one training stages (such as Clarinet, NatrualSpeech), however, the last training stage of
these models are trying to optimize all the parameters through a single network.

In Fig. 1, the latent variable p is called text embeddings which is mis-leading. In fact, p is a latent acoustic representation, because it contains acoustic information such as pitch, duration and energy.

Some important implementation details are missing. As presented in Fig 1, there is a pitch, energy, duration prediction module. How is the phoneme-level pitch, energy and duration obtained and how to predict them? Did you use similar implementation as FastPitch? If so, please state clearly and cite FastPitch.

In introduction, "while all of VITS, FastSpeech 2s and EATS use adversarial training, which is more difficult to converge." This is not correct, both FastSpeech 2S and VITS converge very quickly. For example, VITS only needs to be trained for about 10k steps to have a reasonable output. BTW, the training steps of this model is not reported, however, it is important to specify this to support the authors' claim.

No comparison over the computational cost nor inference speed is presented. It is of particular interest because diffusion models often suffer from higher computational cost. The authors tried to estimate the distance between two latent variables using MSE (shown in equation 27), it is a weird design since the latent variables are of unknown distributions and without any supervision.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The contributions are somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work. Some important details are missing, making it not easy to follow.
content.summary_of_the_review: Several claims are wrong or not well supported, and some important implementation details are missing. The paper is somewhat not easy to follow.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
* Identifies an interesting connection of diffusion-based TTS models to solving the schrodinger bridge problem.
* Presents a generalized version of the SBP to accept conditioning input and variable length.
* Integrates a standard TTS model (FastSpeech-style) with a diffusion vocoder – similar to WaveGrad 2.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths 
* Identifies an interesting connection of diffusion-based TTS models to solving the schrodinger bridge problem.
* Presents a generalized version of the SBP to accept conditioning input and variable length.

# Weaknesses
* Only evaluated on LJSpeech.
* Compares MOS scores rather than performing CMOS tests for closely performing alternative methods.
* Does not compare to diffusion TTS models.
* Does not evaluate the Schron method on other tasks, limiting the relevance to the application area of TTS.
* Uses nearly 2x the parameters of the baseline models to achieve the result.
* Does not clearly describe the difference between this method and current diffusion methods for TTS.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I do not understand the derivation of the solution to the SBP problem and cannot comment on the technical correctness.

I believe the use of the SBP as a TTS vocoder to be novel, though I do not have enough knowledge to tell whether this is just a reframing of an existing method in the terminology of a different problem.

Details about the prosodic text encoder and its training procedure are not provided (as far as I can tell).
content.summary_of_the_review:
I don’t understand the math behind this work – other reviewers will hopefully assess the technical correctness and significance of the new method, especially with respect to prior work such as ItoTTS/ItoWave which looks very similar.

However, the overall structure seems highly similar to a standard two-stage TTS model. There is strong technical novelty in the approach as it appears to be the first application of this problem to the application area of TTS, however this is clearly an applications paper and the overall significance of the empirical result is limited.

Methodologically, the authors compare MOS scores which is not a sensitive enough test for systems with substantially similar performance. As the method is highly related to diffusion models, the authors should compare the work to the current state of the art diffusion models such as WaveGrad 2 or DiffWave – preferably with CMOS (a 7-point side-by-side), not MOS.

The dataset used in the experiments, LJSpeech, is a relatively easy dataset (the MNIST of TTS) – it is difficult to assess the capabilities of the model, in particular the ability to model diverse prosody, from such a limited and small dataset.

The relevance of this method to the ICLR community would be stronger if it was demonstrated on a variety of tasks. I do not think an applications paper has a place at ICLR unless it is an obvious and dramatic improvement of the state of the art in that application – and given the results use MOS, do not compare against other TTS diffusion models, and use a dataset that is relatively boring prosodically, it is very difficult to tell whether this method is substantially better than other methods.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a speech synthesis system based on a conditional version of Schrodinger bridges. It seems to be a two-stage approach where a text-to-mel spectrogram network is trained first; the output of this model is then used as a conditioning signal to a generative model based on Schrodinger bridges on waveform. The authors report state of the art results in term of MOS on LJSpeech. There is an accompanying website with audio examples.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The audio results seem to be of good quality and to be correlated with the MOS. The idea of relying on Schrodinger bridge instead of diffusion models or GANs may be interesting although straightforward.

Weaknesses:
The writing makes the paper too difficult to follow. It is then not easy to evaluate the technical contribution. 
Is the model end-to-end? as it seems that the two components can be trained successively.
The evaluation part is brief, with only a MOS evaluation.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:
I was unable to understand most part of the paper. There is a lack of precision in the definitions (e.g. Sect. 2.1: the definition of Wiener).
The proposed definition of conditional Schrodinger bridge problem of Eq. 4 is puzzling as it seems that the argmin is independant of the text condition j. This is again the case in Eq. 12 and 14, where the conditioning is simply 0

The training scheme is not clear as well. The mel decoder only appears once in the text and once in Fig. 1. Its role is yet to be defined. 
Notations are not intuitive (j for text embedding, gothic M for both text encoder and mel decoder, gothic I for text decoder).


Novelty:
The main novelty lies in relying on the recently proposed generative models based on Schrodinger bridges to implement the vocoder part usually used in text-to-speech models (implemented as GANs or diffusion models in recent applications).

Reproducibility:
Despite the many figures describing the different components, the lack of clarity in the presentation makes it hard to reproduce.
Also, why are the audio examples so close to the ground truth?

Typos:
- mamaner
- waveform instead of wave
content.summary_of_the_review: Even if the authors obtain nice audio results, the paper looks not polished enough to provide reusable insights: many details are left unclear, which makes novelty and importance of the contribution (conditional Schrodinger bridge problem) hard to evaluate.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes an end-to-end (E2E) framework, Schron, based on Schrodinger bridge problem (SBP) for speech waveform synthesis. A two-stage training strategy is proposed. In first stage, text encoder, mel density ratio estimator, and mel score predictor are trained. In second stage, text decoder, mel-encoder, wave density ratio estimator, and wave score predictor are trained. The proposed inference process is also two-stage. In the first stage, noisy wave is firstly generated from Dirac distribution. Then clean waves can be generated from the noisy waves. For baseline models, both two-stage TTS systems and E2E TTS systems are compared in model size and subjective measurement. Higher MOS scores are achieved at the cost of larger model size.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Questions:

(1)	Could the advantage of Schron over the diffusion-based E2E TTS model be explained? Compared to either the discrete Markov chain based or the SDE based diffusion models, Schron seems more complex in theory, training strategy and inference process.

(2)	How many inference steps are used by Schron in waveform generation?

(3)	Could the sample quality of Schron be compared with the diffusion-based models in E2E TTS, e.g., WaveGrad 2 [1] with similar inference time cost?


Others: 

(1) Speech samples on demo page are not normalized.

(2) The subjective evaluation seems not convincing enough to me. The background noise of VITS [2] is apparent on the demo page of Schron, which is not as good as the samples shown in the original work (https://github.com/jaywalnut310/vits ). Moreover, I can feel distinctive gap between the samples generated by Schron and the ground-truth samples, which is not seen in the state-of-the-art E2E TTS systems, e.g., VITS [2] and NaturalSpeech [3]. 


Anonymous issues:

From the demo page, I found the system name is called RealSinger, which is another ICLR paper submission. I am not sure whether this violates the anonymous policy of ICLR, but it will let reviewers know that the two papers may come from the same authors, violating the policy to some degree. 

This also shows the unprofessional experience from authors. How could I trust the paper materials are solid enough if you just copy a demo template from another work but forget to change the system name? 



[1] Nanxin Chen, Yu Zhang, Heiga Zen, Ron J. Weiss, Mohammad Norouzi, Najim Dehak, and William Chan. Wavegrad 2: Iterative refinement for text-to-speech synthesis. In Interspeech, 2021.

[2] Jaehyeon Kim, Jungil Kong, and Juhee Son. Conditional variational autoencoder with adversarial learning for end-to-end text-to-speech. In ICML, 2021

[3] Xu Tan, Jiawei Chen, Haohe Liu, Jian Cong, Chen Zhang, Yanqing Liu, Xi Wang, Yichong Leng, Yuanhao Yi, Lei He, Frank K. Soong, Tao Qin, Sheng Zhao, and Tie-Yan Liu. Naturalspeech: End-to-end text to speech synthesis with human-level quality. arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.04421, 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The author should explain why we need such as a framework, compared to the existing diffusion framework
content.summary_of_the_review: More intuitive explanation and empirical evidence about why we need such a framework are necessary for the acceptance of this work.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
